text: ICANS is not thought to be directly mediated by CAR-T cells themselves.
A chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) is a synthetic transmembrane protein expressed at the surface of immune effector cells that have been reprogrammed either in vitro or in vivo.
With lineage-specific antigens, on-target off-tumour toxicity is common, resulting in depletion of specific cell lineages, or of other cells when antigen expression is aberrant.
In B-ALL, point mutations in CD19 can cause nonfunctional anchoring of the CD19 protein to the cell membrane and consequently loss of surface antigen.

Antigen loss has not been reported so far for alternative myeloma targets such as FCRH5 or GPRC5D, but the authors expect biallelic events causing antigen loss to also be relevant for myeloma targets other than BCMA because myeloma has high frequencies of copy number aberrations including deletions of genes encoding immunotherapy targets.

Allogeneic off-the-shelf CAR-T cells avoid certain limitations of autologous T cells, namely a personalized production process, several weeks of manufacturing time, and the risk of manufacturing failure.

Strategies to reduce TCRαβ activity in allogeneic CAR-T cells include truncated dominant-negative CD3ζ proteins, protein expression blockers, small hairpin RNA, and genome editing with platforms such as ZFNs, meganucleases, TALENs, megaTALs, CRISPR/Cas9, and base editors.
Major barriers to off-the-shelf allogeneic CAR cells are HLA disparity, which results in graft versus host disease and in host-mediated rejection, and these must be addressed.
The primary goal of bridging therapy is to prevent uncontrolled progression of the underlying disease during the manufacturing period before CAR-T cell infusion.
Prior CD19-directed therapy such as blinatumomab is reported as possibly detrimental before CD19 CAR-T cells, particularly through selection of CD19-negative clones, according to accumulating data.
Whether an even more intensive lymphodepleting regimen is needed in solid tumours is currently unknown.
B-cell depletion and the resulting hypogammaglobulinaemia after CD19/CD22 CAR-T therapy are classified as on-target, off-tumour toxicities that may increase the risk of infection.
Profound B cell lymphopenia after CD19 CAR-T cell therapy can result in hypogammaglobulinaemia and absent or impaired vaccine responses that require long-term immunoglobulin replacement therapy.

Flow cytometry detects CAR-T cells either directly with mAbs recognizing the CAR (idiotype, linker region) or a tag in the CAR construct, or indirectly with antigen-Fc chimeric proteins that require a secondary fluorochrome-labelled anti-Fc or anti-biotin mAb.

Under acquire-release ordering, one thread releasing an atomic variable and another thread acquiring the same atomic variable forms a synchronization point that guarantees any prior writes by the releasing thread are visible to the acquiring thread.

In SYCL basic data-parallel kernels, the execution model allows completely parallel execution of work-items but neither guarantees nor requires it, so items may run in any order, including sequentially on a single hardware thread.

Work-items within a work-group are scheduled so that they can cooperate, but they are not required to provide any specific forward progress guarantees, and executing them sequentially between barriers and collectives is a valid implementation.
To use atomic operations with buffers in SYCL, a buffer of non-atomic data is created and transferred to the device, and that data is then accessed through an atomic reference.
While any atomic_ref referencing a specific object exists, all accesses to that object must occur atomically via an instance of atomic_ref.
A Read-after-Write (RAW) dependence occurs when one task needs to read data produced by a different task, and it describes the flow of data between the two kernels.
RAW dependences ensure that data flows in the correct direction between computations, while WAR dependences ensure that existing values are not overwritten before they are read.
A reduction initialized with a buffer or a USM pointer is a scalar reduction operating on the first object in an array, whereas a reduction initialized with a span is an array reduction.
Every SYCL reducer provides a combine() function that combines the partial result from a single work-item with the value of the reduction variable, and its behavior is implementation-defined.

If a device cannot migrate shared allocations on demand, the runtime must conservatively assume a kernel might access any allocation in device-attached memory, so the host and device should not access a shared allocation at the same time and applications should alternate access in phases.

Although shared allocations can migrate, not all SYCL implementations necessarily migrate them; some devices may implement them identically to host allocations, so they remain visible on host and device but may not show the performance gains of migration.
Sub-groups are defined as a core part of the SYCL language so that programmers have a safe alternative to baking in assumptions about execution models that may later prove to be device-specific.

The set of work-items that synchronize at a group_barrier is determined entirely by the group object passed to it, while the optional memory-scope argument only affects the memory operations performed by the barrier, so passing a different scope cannot synchronize more or fewer work-items.

Explicitly requesting an executable-state kernel bundle is effectively free if all kernels were ahead-of-time compiled or were already just-in-time compiled, because all kernels would already be in the executable state.

The semantics of $\mathsf{score}(t)$ is an s-finite kernel even though it need not be a finite kernel, because it is the sum $\sum_{i=0}^\infty k_i$ of kernels $k_i$ that keep the weight when it lies in $[i,i+1)$ and are otherwise 0, each bounded by $i+1$.

The decision problem of whether a probabilistic program terminates in finite expected time on all inputs is $\Pi^0_3$-complete in the arithmetical hierarchy, and thus strictly harder than the universal halting problem for ordinary programs.

A ranking-supermartingale map (RSM-map) with respect to an invariant $I$ is a function $\eta: L\times\mathbb{R}^{|V|}\to\mathbb{R}$ for which there exist $\epsilon>0$ and $K,K'<0$ such that, for all configurations $(\ell,\mathbf{x})$ with $\mathbf{x}\in I(\ell)$: (C1) $\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})\ge 0$ if $\ell\ne\ell_{out}$; (C2) $K\le\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})\le K'$ if $\ell=\ell_{out}$; (C3) $\mathrm{pre}_\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})\le\eta(\ell,\mathbf{x})-\epsilon$ if $\ell\ne\ell_{out}$.
Two sub-distributions $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ over the same set are equal if and only if they are related by the lifting of the equality relation, $\mu_1\,(=)^\sharp\,\mu_2$.

Since any two proper distributions can be coupled by the independent (trivial) coupling $\mu_\times(a_1,a_2)=\mu_1(a_1)\mu_2(a_2)$, the mere existence of a coupling yields little information, and couplings become useful when the joint distribution satisfies additional conditions such as its support satisfying some property.
Because equality on reals is not decidable, the comparison $<$ at type $\mathrm{Real}\to\mathrm{Real}\to\mathrm{Bool}$ cannot have the standard semantics of deciding between $<$ and $\geq$.

In the monadic treatment of QIF, hyper-distributions are the type $\mathbb{D}^2\mathcal{A}$, obtained by applying the distribution monad $\mathbb{D}$ to $\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$ rather than to $\mathcal{A}$, so that QIF programs have type $\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{D}^2\mathcal{A}$ instead of the ordinary probabilistic type $\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{D}\mathcal{A}$.

In the monadic formulation, for a channel $C$ and an uncertainty function $f$ on a prior $\pi$, the uncertainty before is $f\,\pi$ and the uncertainty after observing the output is $(\mu\circ\mathbb{D}f)(C\pi)$, where the multiplication $\mu$ squashes a hyper to a plain distribution by removing all information-flow properties.

Hyper-distributions abstract away the actual values of observations, retaining only the deductions an adversary can make, so that programs such as observing $b$ and observing $(\mathrm{not}\ b)$ are treated as the same, and two programs are behaviourally equal just when their denotations are equal (full abstraction).

A dual-bounded probabilistic region over a state domain $\mathbb{A}$ is a 4-tuple $(a,s,p,m)$ that represents sub-distributions whose support lies within $\gamma(a)$, whose number of support points lies in $[s^{\min},s^{\max}]$, whose probability per support point lies in $[p^{\min},p^{\max}]$, and whose total mass lies in $[m^{\min},m^{\max}]$.

Abstract normalization divides the maximum point bound by the lower mass bound $m^{\min}$ (an under-approximation of total mass) so that the over-approximation $p^{\max}$ of a state's probability remains sound.

If $X\in\gamma(\mathbf{a})$ and the boolean expression $exp$ has non-zero marginal probability in $X$, then the conditioned distribution $X\mid exp$ lies in $\gamma(\mathbf{a}\mid exp)$, which follows from the soundness of abstract conjunction and abstract normalization.

For an unbounded while loop, a variable that is modified unreliably within the loop and has a loop-carried dependence has reliability that decreases monotonically with the number of iterations, so the only sound approximation of its reliability is zero.

Because Rely's analysis considers only the probability that a result is computed fully reliably, it requires only a hardware reliability specification giving the probability that each arithmetic/logical and memory operation executes correctly, is oblivious to the computation's input distribution, and does not require a full model of how soft errors affect its result.

The class of normal monomorphisms of dendroidal sets is the smallest weakly saturated class containing the boundary inclusions $\partial\Omega[T]\to\Omega[T]$ for every tree $T$ in $\Omega$, because every normal monomorphism is a transfinite composition of pushouts of such boundary inclusions.

The equivalence relation on length-labelled trees defining $W(P)$ is generated by three kinds of identification: isomorphisms of trees respecting labellings (including lengths), contraction of edges of length zero, and erasure of vertices labelled by a unit operation.

For trees $S$ and $T$, the map from the coproduct of $\Omega[A]$ over all shuffles $A$ of $S$ and $T$ to $\Omega[S]\otimes\Omega[T]$ is an epimorphism, and the inclusion of each $\Omega[A]$ into $\Omega[S]\otimes\Omega[T]$ is a monomorphism, so the tensor product is a union of the representables of its shuffles.

The subsets $E(A)\subseteq E(S)\times E(T)$ characterizing shuffles correspond only to isomorphism classes of shuffles, so 'the' shuffles of $S$ and $T$ are taken to be those arising from such subsets.

The tensor product of dendroidal sets $\otimes:\mathbf{dSets}\times\mathbf{dSets}\to\mathbf{dSets}$ is the functor, unique up to natural isomorphism, that preserves colimits in each variable separately and on representables is given by $\Omega[S]\otimes\Omega[T]=N(\Omega(S)\otimes\Omega(T))$, the dendroidal nerve of the Boardman–Vogt tensor product of the free operads.

A simplicial set $X$ is an ∞-category (inner Kan complex) if every map $\Lambda^k[n]\to X$ extends to a map $\Delta[n]\to X$ only for the inner horns, i.e. for $n>0$ and $0<k<n$, whereas a Kan complex requires extensions for all $0\le k\le n$.

If $X$ is an inner Kan complex, the homotopy category $\tau(X)$ is isomorphic to the category $\tau_1(X)$ whose objects are the vertices of $X$ and whose arrows $x\to y$ are equivalence classes of 1-simplices $f$ with $d_1f=x$ and $d_0f=y$, where $f\sim f'$ if some 2-simplex $e$ has $d_2e=f$, $d_1e=f'$ and $d_0e=s_0y$.

For a general simplicial set $X$ the category $\tau(X)$ is hard to control because it is defined only by generators and relations, but when $X$ is an inner Kan complex $\tau(X)$ is much easier to describe.

A map of simplicial sets is anodyne if and only if it is a retract of an $\mathcal{I}$-cellular map, where $\mathcal{I}$ is the set of horn inclusions $\Lambda^k[n]\to\Delta[n]$, with analogous statements for inner, left, and right anodyne maps using the corresponding horn inclusions.

For a J-fibration $p: X \to S$ between ∞-categories (or a Kan fibration between general simplicial sets), $p$ is a minimal J-fibration (minimal Kan fibration) if any two fibrewise J-equivalent simplices are equal, where fibrewise J-equivalent n-simplices are those that are fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $\partial\Delta[n]$.

Any fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence over $S$ between two minimal J-fibrations $p:X\to S$ and $q:Y\to S$ of ∞-categories is an isomorphism, and the same holds for minimal Kan fibrations between general simplicial sets.

For a Reedy category R and a map Y→X of E-valued presheaves, the map Y is a Reedy (trivial) fibration if, for each object r of R, the matching map $Y(r)\to Y(\partial r)\times_{X(\partial r)}X(r)$ is a (trivial) fibration in E, where $X(\partial r)$ is the limit of X over strictly positive morphisms into r.

If the projective model structure on each $E^{\mathrm{Aut}(r)}$ exists, the Reedy model structure can still be obtained without E being cofibrantly generated, and in particular when every object of the Reedy category has a trivial automorphism group the cofibrant generation assumption on E becomes redundant, though the resulting structure might not be cofibrantly generated if E is not.

A dendroidal space $X$ is complete if it is local with respect to either of the two endpoint inclusions $\eta \to J$ (viewed as a morphism of discrete dendroidal spaces), i.e. if $\mathrm{Map}(J,X)\to\mathrm{Map}(\eta,X)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

In the Michel–Weinbaum model, the colloid osmotic pressure in the subglycocalyx 'protected region' of the interstitial fluid depends on the solvent filtration rate, so that osmotic forces oppose but, at steady state, do not reverse the filtrate flow.

In the Guytonian framework, venous return (VR) is the flow of blood from the peripheral circulation back to the heart, driven by the gradient between upstream mean systemic pressure (Pms) and downstream right atrial pressure (RAP) and opposed by resistance to venous return (RVR), so that following the Hagen–Poiseuille relation $VR = (Pms - RAP)/RVR$.

A fluid bolus raises venous return and cardiac output only if stressed volume and mean systemic pressure increase significantly with minimal change in right atrial pressure and both ventricles operate on the steep portion of the cardiac function curve.

Pulse pressure variation (PPV), which reflects stroke volume variation, was shown by Michard and colleagues in 2000 to detect fluid responsiveness when it is increased above 12–15% during controlled mechanical ventilation.

In the Stewart physicochemical approach to acid-base balance, plasma [HCO3-] and pH are dependent variables determined by three independent variables: total CO2 content, strong ion difference (SID), and the concentration of weak nonvolatile acids (Atot).

The Stewart approach holds that total CO2 is what ultimately counts only as long as there is sufficient carbonic anhydrase, intact circulation to carry CO2 from tissue to lung, and normally functioning lungs that regulate PaCO2.
The ROSE concept describes four dynamic fluid phases of fluid therapy: resuscitation, optimization, stabilization and evacuation.

Late Goal-Directed Fluid Removal (LGFR), also called de-resuscitation, is defined as active fluid removal with diuretics or renal replacement therapy with net ultrafiltration, started within the first week of ICU stay.
IAH is graded by IAP: grade I is 12 to 15 mmHg, grade II is 15 to 20 mmHg, grade III is 20 to 25 mmHg, and grade IV is above 25 mmHg.

The rise in blood water concentration after a fluid infusion only seems analogous to a drug concentration in pharmacokinetics, because it represents a dilution of the administered water in a much larger water volume, which adds requirements to the calculations.

Volume kinetic analysis has shown that after expansion by a crystalloid fluid the interstitial fluid space is only twice as large as the plasma volume, which is less than commonly assumed, and crystalloid distribution has a half-life of 8 min.

Recent human investigations are reported to confirm animal laboratory evidence that some sodium is stored within the body without commensurate water, contrary to the teaching that body sodium content directly determines extracellular fluid volume.
Immune cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system, including macrophages and dendritic cells, are described as the local sensors of interstitial electrolyte concentration.

In healthy volunteers given a hypertonic saline load after a low-sodium diet, plasma sodium 4 h after infusion had fallen by 1.8 mmol/L against a predicted fall of less than 1 mmol/L, leading the authors to conclude that healthy individuals can osmotically inactivate significant amounts of sodium.
RML is a superset of R2RML that aims to extend R2RML's applicability and broaden its scope by adding support for heterogeneous data.
In RML the iterator (rml:iterator) determines the iteration pattern over the data source and specifies the extract of the data taken during each iteration.

Under the Local-as-View (LAV) approach, data sources are described as views over the global schema, with the mapping rules in $M$ associating a query over the global schema $G$ to each element of the source schema $S$.
A federated query processing system provides a unified access interface to a set of autonomous, distributed, and heterogeneous data sources.

Federated query engines use five join methods: nested loop join, bound-join, hash join, symmetric join, and multiple join; bound-join differs from nested loop join by executing the inner sub-query for a set of bindings rather than for every single binding of the outer intermediate results.

In COMET, a context C is defined as any Boolean expression representing system criteria, i.e., a Boolean function that takes two RDF molecules M1 and M2 and returns true if they are similar according to the system context and false otherwise.

Two RDF molecules $M_G \in \Phi(G)$ and $M_D \in \Phi(D)$ are defined as contextually equivalent iff they satisfy the context, $C(M_1, M_2) = true$, and $Sim_f(M_G, M_D) = \max_{m \in \Phi(D)} Sim_f(M_G, m)$, i.e., they have the highest similarity value.

Knowledge graph embedding models are described as a type of deductive reasoning in vector space that discovers new links, and their vectors are used in downstream tasks such as knowledge graph completion.

The layered perspective, as chosen by the chapter's authors, combines three views of Knowledge Graphs (knowledge representation tools, knowledge management systems, and knowledge application services) as layers: representation of knowledge at the first layer, the management system for that knowledge in the middle, and the application it solves at the top.

According to the authors, achieving a great overall KG system requires taking all layers and their interactions into account, because a good knowledge application platform is hardly possible if the knowledge representation layer is not fit for the purpose.
SANSA DataLake currently supports CSV, Parquet files, Cassandra, MongoDB, Couchbase, ElasticSearch, and various JDBC sources such as MySQL and SQL Server.
Most approaches in SANSA's similarity assessment module are feature-based, which requires the semantic objects to be representable as sets of features.
Hidden Markov Models suit NILM because they model processes with unobservable states, so individual appliance consumption can be estimated from the observable output, the aggregated consumption.

The authors treat question answering, recommender systems, entity resolution and link prediction as application services because they offer a well-defined application, in contrast to a management system that offers a query language supporting such applications.

Every locally finite graph $(V,m;b)$ has a cable system, which can be constructed by adding a loop at every vertex of the simple graph $G_b$ and choosing edge lengths and weights from the weighted degree function and $b$.

A minimal cable system for $(V,m;b)$ need not exist; for example, the combinatorial Laplacian on an infinite path graph $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, which is an antitree with sphere numbers $s_n=1$, has no minimal cable system because the antitree positivity condition fails.

For a non-local Dirichlet form, including graph Laplacians, there is in general no largest intrinsic metric, so no canonical choice of intrinsic metric can be made, whereas for a strongly local Dirichlet form the classical intrinsic metric is in a certain sense the largest and gives a canonical choice.

Markovian uniqueness of a Laplacian means uniqueness of its self-adjoint extensions that enjoy the Markov property, that is, extensions whose heat semigroup $(e^{t\Delta})_{t>0}$ is positivity preserving and $L^\infty$ contractive.

For a non-positive Laplacian, Markovian uniqueness can be restated as follows: the Helmholtz equation $\Delta u=\lambda u$ with $\lambda>0$ admits a unique solution $u\in L^2$ having finite energy, i.e. finite Dirichlet integral $\mathfrak{Q}[u]<\infty$.
Absence of finite volume graph ends does not in general characterize Markovian uniqueness for arbitrary weighted metric graphs $(\mathcal{G},\mu,\nu)$, as already seen for weighted path graphs.

For a finite subgraph $\mathcal K$ of a model, the boundary area $\mathrm{area}(\partial\mathcal K)$ is the sum of $\sqrt{\mu\nu}(e)$ over the edges $e$ of $\mathcal K$ incident to each boundary vertex $v\in\partial\mathcal K$, where $\partial\mathcal K$ consists of the vertices of $\mathcal K$ whose degree in $\mathcal K$ is smaller than their degree in $\mathcal G$.

For a weighted metric graph with a fixed model of finite intrinsic size, if the discrete heat semigroup of a Markovian extension is stochastically complete and the model additionally satisfies $\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\eta(e)\sqrt{|e|\mu(e)}<\infty$, then the corresponding metric-graph heat semigroup is stochastically complete.

A proper extension of a symmetric operator $A$ is an operator $\widetilde A$ with $\mathrm{dom}(A)\subset\mathrm{dom}(\widetilde A)\subset\mathrm{dom}(A^*)$, and the set of all proper extensions is denoted $\mathrm{Ext}(A)$.

For a countable direct sum of boundary triplets $\Pi_j$ for adjoints of symmetric operators $A_j$ with $0<n_+(A_j)=n_-(A_j)\le\infty$, the direct sum $\bigoplus_j\Pi_j$ is a boundary triplet for $A^*=\bigoplus_j A_j^*$ if and only if the maps $\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1$ are bounded from $\mathrm{dom}(A^*)$ with the graph norm to $\mathcal{H}$, equivalently if and only if $\sup_j(\|M_j(\mathrm{i})\|+\|(\mathrm{Im}\,M_j(\mathrm{i}))^{-1}\|)<\infty$; the direct sum need not be a boundary triplet automatically.

Under the finite intrinsic size assumption (which guarantees the net property), the metric graph $(\mathcal{G},\varrho_\eta)$ and its vertex set $(\mathcal{V},\varrho_{\mathcal V})$ are quasi-isometric, which connects their large-scale properties.

The strong/weak Liouville property (all positive/bounded harmonic functions are constant) is not preserved under bi-Lipschitz maps in general, yet the authors state that the equivalence holds in their setting of the metric graph and its vertex set, without any additional local conditions such as bounded geometry.

The traditional definition of the Siegel operator at the $J$-cusp chooses a 0-dimensional cusp $I\subset J$, takes the $I$-trivialization and coordinates $(\tau,z,w)$, and sets $(\Phi_J f)(\tau)=\lim_{t\to\infty} f(\tau,0,it)$ for $\tau\in\mathbb{H}$, which is easy to define but requires checking modularity and the reduced weight afterwards.

The Siegel operator $M_{\lambda,k}(\Gamma)\to S_{\lambda_1+k}(\Gamma_J)\otimes V(J)_{\lambda'}$ is in general not surjective, because modular forms are invariant under the full stabilizer $\Gamma(J)^*_{\mathbb{Z}}$ of $J$ and not only $\Gamma(J)_{\mathbb{Z}}$, so its image lies in the $G$-invariant part with $G=\Gamma_J^*/\Gamma_J$.

The canonical extension of $\mathcal{E}_{\lambda,k}$ over $\overline{\mathcal{X}(J)}$ does not depend on the choice of the rank 1 primitive sublattice $I\subset J$, because the transition between the $I$- and $I'$-trivializations is a $GL$-valued holomorphic function that is constant on each fiber of $\mathcal{X}(J)\to\mathcal{V}_J$ and hence extends holomorphically over $\overline{\mathcal{X}(J)}$.

Although the canonical extension over $\overline{\mathcal{X}(J)}$ retains a trivialization by construction, this no longer holds on the full toroidal compactifications, since around $\Delta_J$ one must further take the quotient by $\overline{\Gamma(J)}_\mathbb{Z}$, which does not preserve the trivialization.

A Jacobi form of weight $(\lambda,k)$ and index $m$ for the integral Jacobi group $\overline{\Gamma(J)}_{\mathbb Z}$ is a $\overline{\Gamma(J)}_{\mathbb Z}$-invariant section of $\mathcal{E}_{\lambda,k}\otimes\Theta_J^{\otimes m}$ over $\Delta_J$ that is holomorphic at every cusp $I\subset J$ of $\mathbb{H}_J$ (the space is denoted $J_{\lambda,k,m}(\Gamma(J)_{\mathbb Z})$).

For $\lambda\neq\det$, there is an injective map $J_{\lambda,k,m}(\Gamma(J)_{\mathbb Z})\hookrightarrow\bigoplus_{r=-\lambda_1}^{\lambda_1}J_{k+r,m}(\Gamma(J)_{\mathbb Z})^{\oplus\alpha(r)}$, where $\alpha(r)$ is the rank of $\mathrm{Gr}^r\mathcal{E}_\lambda$, so vector-valued Jacobi forms decompose into tuples of scalar-valued Jacobi forms of various weights.

For $\lambda\neq\det$, the space $J_{\lambda,k,m}(\Gamma(J)_{\mathbb{Z}})$ is zero when $k+\lambda_1<n/2-1$, because every weight $k+r$ in the decomposition satisfies $k+r\le k+\lambda_1<n/2-1$ and scalar-valued Jacobi forms vanish in that weight range.

The embedding of $J_{\lambda,k,m}(\Gamma(J)_{\mathbb Z})$ into a sum of scalar-valued Jacobi form spaces is not canonical, since it requires a choice of splitting of the filtration on the space of Jacobi forms, although the last (level $\lambda_1$) subspace is canonically determined.

On the tube domain $\mathcal D_I$, for $v_1,v_2\in V(I)_{\mathbb R}$ the Petersson pairing of the distinguished sections of $\mathcal E$ is $(s_{v_1}(Z),s_{v_2}(Z))_{\mathcal E}=-(v_1,v_2)+\frac{2(v_1,\mathrm{Im}Z)(v_2,\mathrm{Im}Z)}{(\mathrm{Im}Z,\mathrm{Im}Z)}$, with $(\,,)$ the natural quadratic form on $V(I)_{\mathbb R}\simeq U(I)_{\mathbb R}$.

The vanishing of holomorphic tensors for $0<k<n/2-1$ follows by embedding $H^0(X,(\Omega^1_X)^{\otimes k})$ into a direct sum of spaces $M_{\lambda(\alpha),k}(\Gamma)$ over the irreducible summands of $\mathrm{St}^{\otimes k}$: summands with $\lambda(\alpha)\neq 1,\det$ vanish for $k<n/2$, the determinant character does not occur for $k<n$, and the trivial summand gives scalar forms $M_k(\Gamma)=0$ for $0<k<n/2-1$.

For a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n)$ of an irreducible representation of $O(n,\mathbb{C})$ with $\lambda\neq 1,\det$, $\mathrm{corank}(\lambda)$ is defined as the maximal index $1\le i\le [n/2]$ such that $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\cdots=\lambda_i$ and $\lambda_n=\lambda_{n-1}=\cdots=\lambda_{n+1-i}=0$.

For a nontrivial highest weight $\rho$ of $SO(n,\mathbb{C})$ (with $\rho_1\neq0$) and $\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}$, the irreducible highest weight module $L(\rho,\alpha)$ is unitarizable if and only if $-\alpha\ge n+\rho_1-\mathrm{corank}(\rho)-1$, and the vanishing proof uses only the "only if" direction.
In cultured cortical neurons, nicotine-induced Akt phosphorylation was blocked by the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 but not by the MEK inhibitor PD98059, indicating that PI3K rather than MAPK is involved.

The Src tyrosine kinase inhibitor reduced Akt phosphorylation, and PI3K and Fyn were physically associated with α7 nAChRs, which the authors take to suggest that nAChR stimulation causes Akt phosphorylation through signal transduction from Fyn to PI3K.

Although α4β2 nAChR stimulation also protected against Aβ- and glutamate-induced cytotoxicity, this protection was not inhibited by LY294002, suggesting that the PI3K system is not directly involved in α4β2 nAChR-mediated neuroprotection.
Long-term tobacco smoking or nicotine application induces up-regulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), which in most cases also facilitates their functions.

In cortical neuron cultures, the increase in nAChR protein caused by long-term donepezil treatment was suppressed by simultaneous treatment with the α7-nAChR antagonist MLA, the PI3K inhibitor LY294002, or the MAPKK inhibitor PD98059, indicating that nAChR, PI3K and MAPK pathways are involved in the up-regulation.

The authors report that donepezil lacked protection when applied simultaneously with glutamate and acted in a manner dependent on pretreatment duration and concentration, which they say strongly suggests a mechanism other than AChE inhibition.
[3H]ACh uptake into brain segments has been confirmed to be active and to depend on time and temperature.

Lower HC-3 concentrations (0.1–1 μM) that selectively inhibit the high-affinity choline transporter CHT1 but not ACh uptake failed to increase evoked [3H]efflux, suggesting that the HC-3 effect arises from inhibited ACh uptake rather than choline uptake and that ACh-derived choline may not be significantly transported back into cholinergic terminals, which challenges the classical choline recycling view.
CaMKII activation is crucial for nicotine-induced GLAST expression and glutamate transport in cortical microglia, since inhibiting CaMKII blocks both effects.

In cultured rat microglia, galantamine and nicotine significantly enhanced Aβ phagocytosis in Ca2+-containing medium but not in Ca2+-free medium, whereas baseline phagocytosis without either drug was almost the same in both media.

In cultured mouse neurons, Shati/Nat8l overexpression induced axonal growth but not dendrite elongation and increased ATP content, and the authors suggest that neuronal Shati/Nat8l induces axon outgrowth via ATP synthesis independently of mGluR3 signaling.
Virtually all experimental ischemia studies reporting deleterious effects of nicotine used continuous delivery by osmotic pumps or repeated daily administration at relatively high doses.
What is the underlying cause of cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and in what clinical setting is it particularly seen?

Which combination of factors appears to be associated with a higher risk of cytokine release syndrome after CAR-T cell therapy? A) High tumour burden and low CAR-T cell dose B) High tumour burden and prior tocilizumab prophylaxis C) Low tumour burden and high CAR-T cell dose D) High tumour burden and high CAR-T cell dose
What speech and writing changes are prominent early features of ICANS, and what can they progress to if the syndrome worsens?
What is the proposed mechanism by which inflammatory cytokines are thought to cause ICANS?

A patient on day 4 after CAR-T infusion has a fully normal ICE score of 10, is awake, has no seizures, and shows no raised intracranial pressure, but has marked myoclonus. The team assigns grade 3 ICANS on the basis of the myoclonus. Is it correct that this myoclonus determines the ICANS grade? (Yes/No)

A research group describes an early CAR construct. It contains an extracellular scFv that recognizes a tumour antigen, a transmembrane region, and an intracellular portion made of the CD3 zeta signalling domain plus the intracellular domain of CD28 as a costimulatory domain. Is this construct a first generation CAR? (Yes/No)

In a CAR construct, a segment spans the cell membrane and connects the extracellular scFv to the intracellular CD3 zeta domain. Changing this segment alters the flexibility and conformation of the receptor and how efficiently it binds its target epitope. Is this segment functioning as the transmembrane region of the CAR? (Yes/No)

A research group designs a receptor-based T cell therapy against a tumour. The receptor recognises a short peptide only when it is presented in a specific polymorphic HLA allele on the target cell surface, so patients lacking that allele cannot be treated. Does this receptor behave like a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) in its mode of target recognition? (Yes/No)
What are the limitations of dual-antigen targeting for CAR-T cells in terms of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) risk and on-target off-tumour and off-target off-tumour toxicity?

A research group builds allogeneic CAR-T cells and uses TALEN genome editing to knock out CD52 in them. The goal is to let the cells survive anti-CD52 antibody treatment. They do not target the TCR, CD3ζ, or any TCRαβ-related component. Is this an example of a strategy to reduce TCRαβ activity in allogeneic CAR-T cells? (Yes/No)

In a single-centre phase 1 trial of CD19 CAR-T cells in relapsed/refractory adult ALL, what was observed regarding disease burden changes during the bridging period? A) Reductions in disease burden during bridging were associated with unfavourable outcomes after CAR-T therapy. B) Increases in disease burden during bridging were associated with favourable outcomes after CAR-T therapy. C) Reductions in disease burden during bridging were not associated with any difference in outcomes after CAR-T therapy. D) Reductions in disease burden during bridging were associated with favourable outcomes after CAR-T therapy.
Why may prior CD19-directed therapy, such as blinatumomab, be detrimental before CD19 CAR-T cell therapy?
